According to an information note issued by the Turkish Medical Association (Türk Tabipleri Birliği) in June 2013, CS (chlorobenzylidenemalononitrile) and CN (chloroacetophenone) gases are used by law-enforcement officials in Turkey.

According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, CS and CN gases damage the eyes, cause burns on the skin, severely affect the respiratory system and the lungs, restrict breathing, slow down the heart beat and cause fluctuations in blood pressure.

According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, prolonged contact with CS and CN gases permanently damages the cornea of the eye, upsets the heart rhythm, and has caused damage to the lungs which has led to deaths.

According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, the effects of CS and CN gases are more pronounced in children, pregnant women and persons with existing respiratory problems, heart problems, aneurysms, allergies and weak immune systems.

According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, sudden allergic oedema caused in the upper respiratory systems by CS and CN gases, as well as use of gases on persons with asthma or bronchitis, may be fatal.

On 3 June 2013 the Respiratory Society of Turkey (Türkiye Solunum Araştırmaları Derneği; TÜSAD) issued a press release to inform the public about the dangers of tear gas and about the steps to be taken after contact with tear gas.
According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, tear gas affects primarily the mucus membranes, in particular the eyes, throat, respiratory system and the nose.

According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, on contact tear gas immediately causes a general feeling of burning; discomfort and excessive watering of the eyes; pain and a feeling of burning of the skin and in the nose and throat; coughing; breathing difficulties; extreme restlessness and discomfort; and temporary blindness.

According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, although tear gas does not cause permanent damage in the organs with which it comes into contact, its acute effects are extremely discomforting and lead to panic.

Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that assistance and medical aid are rendered to any injured or affected persons at the earliest possible moment.

Principle 12 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that as everyone is allowed to participate in lawful and peaceful assemblies, Governments and law enforcement agencies and officials shall recognize that force and firearms may be used only in accordance with Principles 13 and 14.

Principle 13 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that in the dispersal of assemblies that are unlawful but non-violent, law enforcement officials shall avoid the use of force or, where that is not practicable, shall restrict such force to the minimum extent necessary.

Principle 14 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that in the dispersal of violent assemblies, law enforcement officials may use firearms only when less dangerous means are not practicable and only to the minimum extent necessary, and shall not use firearms except under the conditions stipulated in Principle 9.

Paragraph 35 of the Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, Maina Kiai (UN Human Rights Council A/HRC/20/27, 21 May 2012) recalls that tear gas does not discriminate between demonstrators and non-demonstrators, healthy people and people with health conditions.
The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (the CPT) has expressed its concerns over the use of pepper spray in law enforcement.
The CPT considers that pepper spray is a potentially dangerous substance and should not be used in confined spaces (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).

The CPT considers that even when pepper spray is used in open spaces it has serious reservations, and that if exceptionally it needs to be used, there should be clearly defined safeguards in place, including that persons exposed to pepper spray should be granted immediate access to a medical doctor and be offered an antidote (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).
The CPT considers that pepper spray should never be deployed against a prisoner who has already been brought under control (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that while public demonstrations in Turkey are subject to fewer restrictions than in the past, a number of incidents have raised concerns, and that in several regions brutality by the security forces has been alleged in the context of demonstrations and outdoor NGO press statements.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that during the demonstration marking international Women's Day in Istanbul on 6 March 2005, police intervened with disproportionate force, using tear gas and truncheons and injuring a number of participants.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that the Turkish government quickly conveyed the message that such behaviour on the part of the police is unacceptable following the incident of 6 March 2005.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that following the incident of 6 March 2005, the Ministry of Interior demoted and fined 6 policemen and reprimanded 3 senior officials.
An expert was appointed by the domestic investigating authorities to examine the video footage of the events of 6 March 2005 and prepare a report.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, police officers had not issued any warnings to the demonstrators to disperse before attacking them on 6 March 2005.
According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, the demonstrators had not resisted the police intervention on 6 March 2005.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, the demonstrators had not attacked the police on 6 March 2005 but had simply tried to run away from the area.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, police had hit the demonstrators — including those who had fallen to the ground — with their truncheons, kicked them, punched them and sprayed them with tear gas on 6 March 2005.
On 8 March 2005 the applicant submitted a written request to the Bakırköy prosecutor requesting a medical examination.
The applicant alleged in her written request to the Bakırköy prosecutor that excessive force had been used by the police officers during the incident on 6 March 2005.
The Bakırköy prosecutor referred the applicant to the Forensic Medicine Institute for a medical examination.
A medical examination of the applicant was carried out on 8 March 2005 at the Bakırköy branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute.

According to the report of the medical examination carried out at the Bakırköy branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute on 8 March 2005, a large number of ecchymosed areas of various sizes were present on the applicant's body, including her left upper arm, right forearm, left femur, buttocks and knees.

The doctor who conducted the medical examination at the Bakırköy branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute on 8 March 2005 concluded that the applicant's injuries would prevent her from working for a period of five days.
On 11 March 2005 the applicant lodged an official complaint with the Istanbul prosecutor against the Governor of Istanbul and the police officers responsible for her ill-treatment.

In her complaint to the Istanbul prosecutor, the applicant requested, inter alia, that the Governor of Istanbul and the police chiefs who abused their duties by not allowing her to enjoy her right to assembly be put on trial.
In her complaint to the Istanbul prosecutor, the applicant requested that the police officers who had ill-treated her be put on trial.
On 8 April 2005 the Chief Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation concluded that the applicant had not mentioned a specific incident that could be attributed to the Governor of Istanbul.
On 8 April 2005 a decision was made not to prosecute the Governor of Istanbul.
On 6 June 2005 the disciplinary board of the police considered that six police officers had kicked the demonstrators and had also hit them with their truncheons during the incident of 6 March 2005.
The disciplinary board of the police held that the six police officers' actions during the incident of 6 March 2005 amounted to 'degrading behaviour'.
The disciplinary board of the police decided to 'condemn' the actions of three police chiefs for failing to train the six police officers properly.

The disciplinary board of the police imposed a fine equivalent to three days' salary on the six police officers who had kicked the demonstrators and hit them with their truncheons during the incident of 6 March 2005.

On 12 December 2005 the Istanbul prosecutor decided not to bring criminal proceedings against forty-four police officers for the offence of abuse of duty in respect of victims and complainants whose bodies did not bear any injuries.
In the Istanbul prosecutor's decision of 12 December 2005, thirty-nine persons, including the applicant, were named as victims and complainants.

The applicant lodged an objection against the Istanbul prosecutor's decision of 12 December 2005 not to bring criminal proceedings against forty-four police officers, in which she repeated her complaints about the excessive use of force against her.
The applicant's objection against the Istanbul prosecutor's decision of 12 December 2005 was rejected on 28 September 2007 by the Beyoğlu Assize Court.

On 9 December 2005 the Istanbul prosecutor filed an indictment with the Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance accusing a total of fifty-four police officers of the offence of causing injuries by exceeding the limits of their powers on the use of force.
In the indictment filed on 9 December 2005, forty-nine persons, including the applicant, were listed as victims and complainants.

The indictment filed on 9 December 2005 made references to a report which had been forwarded to the Istanbul prosecutor on 28 April 2005 pertaining to an investigation conducted by four senior police inspectors in the immediate aftermath of the events of 6 March 2005.

According to the indictment filed on 9 December 2005, the inspectors' report concluded that seven of the fifty-four police officers named as suspects in the indictment had used excessive force against fifteen of the complainants and victims, including the applicant.
According to the indictment filed on 9 December 2005, the four senior police inspectors considered that the seven officers had not used their truncheons in accordance with the applicable regulations.

According to the indictment filed on 9 December 2005, the four senior police inspectors considered that the seven officers had kicked a number of female demonstrators who had already been neutralised.
The trial before the Fourth Division of the Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance began in 2005.
The trial before the Fourth Division of the Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance was concluded on 12 May 2011.
Six of the defendant police officers accepted during the preliminary investigation stage that they had kicked the demonstrators from behind.

The lawyers defending the six defendant police officers submitted during the trial that the self-implicating statements had been taken from the police officers by the inspectors under duress and as a result of the press coverage of the incidents.
The lawyers defending the six defendant police officers submitted during the trial that the inspectors questioning the police officers had acted contrary to the applicable procedure.

The defendant police officers maintained before the trial court that the medical reports, while establishing that the incidents had taken place, were insufficient to establish the identities of the police officers, and that the victims should have been required to identify them first.
The defendant police officers maintained before the trial court that the offences in question were time-barred and the proceedings against them should have been discontinued.

In his final submissions during the trial, the prosecutor agreed with the defendants and argued that the defendants should be acquitted because the victims had been unable to identify the police officers.

The trial court found that the defendants' objections based on the statute of limitations should be rejected, as proceedings against them would be time-barred five years after the last defence submissions were made by them on 8 September 2006.
The trial court noted that the large numbers of defendants and victims, coupled with the fact that this was a large-scale incident, resulted in delays in obtaining all the evidence.
The trial court noted that the trial was also delayed as a result of the defendants' covering their faces with helmets and not displaying their identification numbers.

The trial court found, having examined the video footage of the events as well as the reports and witness statements, that it was not possible to expect the victims to identify the police officers who attacked them because it was not possible to recognise the police officers in the video footage.

The inspectors who had questioned the police officers were heard in the course of the trial proceedings and confirmed the authenticity and accuracy of the statements they had taken from the police officers.

The trial court found that the inspectors' statements were corroborated by the video footage which shows the punching, kicking, hitting with truncheons and shields, and using an excessive amount of tear gas.

The trial court found, based on statements taken from the police officers by the inspectors, that defendants M.C. and A.O.P. had kicked from behind two female demonstrators who had in their hands nothing to pose a danger to the two officers.
The trial court found, based on statements taken from the police officers by the inspectors, that defendant S.B. used excessive force against a woman who had taken refuge in a café.
The trial court found, based on statements taken from the police officers by the inspectors, that defendant C.U. hit a female demonstrator on her shoulder and broke one of her bones.

The trial court found, based on statements taken from the police officers by the inspectors, that defendant Y.K. kicked a demonstrator who had been trying to seek help from the police after having been sprayed with tear gas.
The trial court found, based on statements taken from the police officers by the inspectors, that defendant E.B. kicked a person who had already been arrested.
The trial court found that some of the defendant police officers exceeded the limits of their powers on the use of force and used excessive force.

The trial court concluded that police officers M.C., A.O.P., S.B., Y.K. and E.B. had used excessive force against the demonstrators and committed the offence of ill-treatment defined in section 245 of the Criminal Code then in force (Law No. 765).
The trial court sentenced police officers M.C., A.O.P., S.B., Y.K. and E.B. to terms of imprisonment ranging from five to ten months.

The trial court found police officer C.U. guilty of the offence of causing grievous bodily harm while using his powers as a public official, an offence defined in section 86 § 3 of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237), for having broken a bone of one of the demonstrators.
The trial court sentenced police officer C.U. to twenty-one months' imprisonment.
The remaining forty-eight defendant police officers were acquitted by the trial court for lack of evidence.

According to information provided to the Court by the Government on 10 November 2011, the criminal proceedings against the police officers were discontinued on 8 September 2011 on account of the statute of limitations.

Section 245 of the Criminal Code in force at the material time (Law No. 765) provided that any law-enforcement officer who, in the course of duty and in circumstances other than those prescribed by law, ill-treats, injures or hits a person or inflicts on them bodily harm, shall be sentenced to between three months' and five years' imprisonment and temporarily barred from public service.

Section 86(1) of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237) provides that a person who intentionally causes physical suffering to another person, or harms that other person's physical or mental health, shall be sentenced to between one and three years' imprisonment.

Section 86(2)(c) of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237) provides that if the offence of intentionally causing bodily harm is committed by virtue of execution of public duties, the offender shall be prosecuted without waiting for an official complaint from the victim and sentenced to between two and five years' imprisonment.

Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that assistance and medical aid are rendered to any injured or affected persons at the earliest possible moment.

Paragraph 16 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Denmark (CAT/C/DNK/CO/5, 16 July 2007) recommends that Denmark review the existing framework to handle allegations of excessive use of force by law enforcement officials to ensure its compliance with the Convention against Torture.

Paragraph 16 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Denmark (CAT/C/DNK/CO/5, 16 July 2007) recommends that Denmark ensure prompt and impartial investigations into all complaints or allegations of misconduct, in particular when a person dies or is seriously injured following contact with law enforcement officials.

Paragraph 16 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Denmark (CAT/C/DNK/CO/5, 16 July 2007) recommends that Denmark review and strengthen its education and training programmes relating to the use of force by law enforcement officials to ensure that the use of force is strictly limited to that required to perform their duties.

Paragraph 13 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Turkey (CAT/C/TUR/CO/3, 20 January 2011) notes the acknowledgement by the representative of Turkey of excessive use of force by law enforcement authorities and information on measures taken to eradicate such practice, including by inscribing identification numbers on the helmet of police officers during demonstrations.

Paragraph 13 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Turkey (CAT/C/TUR/CO/3, 20 January 2011) states that the Committee remains concerned at reports indicating an increase in the excessive use of force and ill-treatment of demonstrators by police outside official detention places.

Paragraph 13 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Turkey (CAT/C/TUR/CO/3, 20 January 2011) recommends that Turkey promptly implement effective measures to put an end to excessive use of force and ill-treatment by law enforcement authorities.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that following the incident of 6 March 2005, the Ministry of Interior demoted and fined 6 policemen and reprimanded 3 senior officials.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that a judicial investigation launched by the Istanbul Public Prosecutor following the incident of 6 March 2005 was ongoing at the time of the report.
